name: Maay
confidence_why: The only first-hand description of Lower Jubba Maay, Paster 2006 (repeated in Comfort and Paster 2009), gives weak root-final stress and no tone from a single consultant, while Saeed 1982 describes the Baydhaba dialect as tonal with high tone mostly on the noun's last syllable, a dialect difference that Paster addresses and that agrees on final placement, so the record rests on one source with no contradiction for its own dialect. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Paster 2006.

catalog_quote: However, no such effects of tone or accent are found in LJM. Stress is root-final, but it is not very prominent and is often not distinguishable at all, and the pitch profile of words is predictable based on the number and shape of syllables in the word and the position of the word in the sentence. Saeed (1982: 9) shows that in Central Somali (CS), tone is contrastive on noun roots. According to Saeed, most nouns have final high tone, while some disyllabic roots have initial high tone. As seen in the examples below, both patterns correspond to final stress in LJM. ... In monosyllables, CS contrasts high vs. low tone. There is no such contrast in LJM; all monosyllables are produced with the same kind of word stress. ... audit.recode_to: Either (a) split/annotate by dialect: keep 'morphological' (weak root-final stress, no tone) explicitly for Lower Jubba Maay (Paster 2006; Comfort & Paster 2009) and add that Bay-region/Baydhaba Maay ('Central Somali', Saeed 1982 sec. 2.5) has a Somali-type tonal accent -- one H per word; nouns mostly final-H, a lexical set of disyllables initial-H, monosyllables H=masc vs L=fem; verb paradigms with characteristic tone patterns; tonal subject marking -- which under this catalog's conventions (Somali soma1255 coded 'tonal' from Hyman 1981) would be 'tonal'; or (b) if one code must stand for maay1238, reclassify as 'tonal' with a caution that the Lower Jubba dialect has lost the accentual contrasts (Paster 2006: 79). At minimum the the primary-stress rule sentence 'No lexical tone or contrastive stress' must be restricted to LJM and a caution added.

sources.citation: Saeed, John I. 1982. Central Somali: A grammatical outline. Afroasiatic Linguistics 8(2): 77-119 [issue pp. 1-43]. Malibu: Undena.
sources.quote: 'Central Somali has three phonological tones: a basic high tone versus low tone opposition and a high to low falling tone found over long syllables in some verb forms. Usually only one syllable has high tone, and all polysyllables were found to have one syllable with high tone... This tone opposition could possibly be described in terms of accent or stress. Prominent syllables are higher in pitch, slightly longer ... and louder.' Nouns of 3-4 syllables and most disyllables: H on last syllable (osbá 'salt', boodá 'thigh', dilmaañá 'mosquito'); a small set of disyllables initial H (fárow 'zebra'
sources.locator: sec. 1 Introduction pp. 2-3 (AAL 8: 78-79: Baydhaba/Bur Hakaba dialect, 'Central Somali (Rahanwin, Af Maymay)', not mutually intelligible with Common or Benaadir Somali); sec. 2.5 Tone pp. 8-11 (AAL 8: 84-86); sec. 5.3 yes-no questions (stress on low-toned question suffix)
sources.note: Primary description of heartland (Bay region/Baydhaba, 'Af Maymay') Maay by a Somali specialist working with multiple speakers; sec. 2.5 documents a Somali-type tonal accent with lexical (noun class, gender on monosyllables) and grammatical (verb paradigm, subject case) contrasts, directly contradicting the record's languoid-level clause 'No lexical tone or contrastive stress', which rests on one Lower Jubba diaspora speaker. downloaded now.

sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: These data and generalizations strongly suggest that KM has a restricted tonal system. The language exhibits a privative tonal contrast between H and toneless stems. High tone is predictably assigned to underlyingly toneless stems based on stem shape and the presence vs. absence of modifiers of different types. High tone is also obligatory on all content words (i.e., nouns and verbs), except in one syntactic context, namely on post-verbal objects, regardless of their focus status. [...] Despite the fact that a H may appear on a stem in some contexts, or on a modifier in others, there are never any instances in which a H appears on both at once. In this way, H in KM is culminative in all contexts that we have explored.

sources.note: Catalog codes maay1238 as classification morphological, tone_cls=no-tone on Paster 2006 (Lower Jubba Maay). This work describes Kenyan Maay first-hand as a restricted (but 'definitionally tonal') tone system: privative H vs toneless stems; H location diagnostic of noun gender (masculine H on final vocalic mora of stem, e.g. gaal 'camel' H on final mora with rising contour; feminine H on penultimate vocalic mora in isolation, e.g. bilaŋ 'woman'; monosyllabic CVC nouns of both genders carry H), Tables 1-6, pp. 274-277.
